tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

tools.name: ToolSearch
tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

tools.name: Workflow
tools.description:
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a system-reminder confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a system-reminder confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.
- The user directly asked you to run a workflow or use multi-agent orchestration in their own words ("use a workflow", "run a workflow", "fan out agents", "orchestrate this with subagents"). The ask must be in the user's words — a task that would merely benefit from a workflow does not count.
- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.

The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

Before writing a script, load the `workflow-authoring` skill — the workflow authoring reference: script API and gotchas, resume, the **Ultracode** section, quality patterns, worked examples.

This session has the default workflow size guideline: medium — keep workflows under 10 agents. This is a guideline, not a hard limit — follow it unless the user's prompt calls for a different scale. The user can raise or remove it with "Dynamic workflow size" in /config.

content.text:
The frontend uses **Geist** for nearly all text, plus three other fonts with smaller jobs. They're set in `frontend/src/index.css:50-53` and loaded in `frontend/src/main.tsx:4-7`.

| Token | Font | Where it shows up |
|---|---|---|
| `--font-sans` | **Geist Variable** | All body text |
| `--font-heading` | **Geist Variable** | Headings (the same font as the body) |
| `--font-brand` | **Sora 600** | The "Motus" wordmark: sidebar, page header, landing |
| `--font-serif-display` | **Instrument Serif Italic** | Accent words on the landing page |
| (none) | **Geist Mono Variable** | Only in the ASCII background in `background.tsx` |

**A bug worth fixing first:** Geist Mono gets loaded, but the `font-mono` class doesn't use it. `@theme` has no `--font-mono`, so `font-mono` (used in `chart.tsx` and elsewhere) falls back to the system monospace font. Adding one line fixes it:

```css
--font-mono: "Geist Mono Variable", ui-monospace, monospace;
```

## Should you change it?

Geist is already a good choice for a clinical dashboard. It's neutral, easy to read on a laptop at arm's length, and supports `tabular-nums`. Replacing it now probably won't help much. Two smaller changes would do more:

1. **Make headings look different from body text.** Right now `--font-heading` is the same as `--font-sans`, so headings only stand out by size and weight.
2. **Cut down the number of fonts.** Four families is a lot for one product, and Sora is loaded only for one wordmark.

## Alternatives, if you do want a change

**Body (to replace Geist):**
- **Inter**: the safe choice. Excellent numerals and a large set of OpenType features, but it looks generic.
- **IBM Plex Sans**: technical and medical in feel. It comes with Plex Mono and Plex Serif, so one family could cover all three roles.
- **Public Sans**: plain and institutional, close to a government health-service look. It reads as trustworthy.

**Headings (separate from the body):**
- **Instrument Serif**, which is already loaded. Using it for page titles costs nothing extra and makes the landing page and dashboard look like one product.
- **Newsreader** or **Source Serif 4**: an editorial, research-paper tone that suits "clinical receipt" content.
- **Fraunces**: warmer and more distinctive, but it can look playful for an ALS product.

**Mono (for numbers and readouts):**
- Keep **Geist Mono**, just map it properly as above.
- **JetBrains Mono** or **IBM Plex Mono** are the alternatives if you switch body fonts.

## My recommendation, given it's demo day

Keep Geist and add the `--font-mono` line. Then try Instrument Serif on `--font-heading` for page titles only, since it's already loaded and needs no new dependency. If you'd rather drop a font family, swap the Sora wordmark for Geist semibold with tight tracking.

I can make the mono fix and the heading swap now if you want. It's about a 3-line change in `index.css`.

I couldn't check which Callio Labs components use the two brand fonts. GitHub's code search needs a login, and `gh` isn't installed here.

If that's what you want for Motus, the easiest change is to swap the Sora wordmark for Chillax Semibold: copy the `.woff2` into `frontend/public/` and add one `@font-face`. That takes about 5 minutes and doesn't add a dependency. I can do it now if you want.

content.text:
The site has a warm paper background, navy ink, teal accents and a lowercase "addo labs" wordmark over an italic serif tagline. It feels editorial and scientific, like a lab notebook, more than a typical tech startup. These fonts would push that further. All are free for commercial use.

## Wordmark (replacing Sora)

The word is mostly round letters (a, d, o, plus "dd"), so it suits fonts with distinctive round shapes.

| Font | Source | Why it fits |
|---|---|---|
| **Fraunces** (Soft axis up) | Google · `@fontsource-variable/fraunces` | A soft, warm serif that looks very good lowercase on paper. It's the most distinctive option and leans into the lab-notebook feel. |
| **General Sans** | Fontshare (self-host) | Same foundry as Chillax, so it's closest to the Callio Labs feel, but calmer and more clinical. |
| **Bricolage Grotesque** | Google · `@fontsource-variable/bricolage-grotesque` | A grotesque with some quirks and noticeable personality at large sizes. It's modern without looking like every other SaaS site. |
| **Zodiak** | Fontshare (self-host) | A sharp, high-contrast serif. Reads as "journal" or "publication", which suits drug discovery. |

## Tagline / accent (currently Instrument Serif Italic)

- **Newsreader Italic**: like a research paper. It holds up at small sizes better than Instrument Serif.
- **Gambetta Italic** (Fontshare): warmer and more literary.
- Or keep Instrument Serif. It already fits, and it's the strongest part of the current setup.

## Data and readouts (Geist Mono today)

- **Martian Mono**: wide and technical, like lab-instrument output. Distinctive for scores and compound IDs.
- **IBM Plex Mono**: the reliable scientific choice, very legible.
- **JetBrains Mono**: neutral, and easy to read at arm's length.

## Body text

I'd keep **Geist**. Body text should stay unremarkable. If you want a warmer alternative, **Instrument Sans** or **Hanken Grotesk** both go well with the serifs above.

## Two complete pairings

1. **Lab notebook**: Fraunces wordmark, Instrument Serif tagline, Geist body, Martian Mono data. Warm, editorial and the most memorable at an expo table.
2. **Quiet precision**: General Sans wordmark, Newsreader tagline, Geist body, IBM Plex Mono data. Calmer and more clinical, and closest to Callio Labs.

**I recommend the lab-notebook pairing.** Fraunces and Martian Mono are both on npm, so it's two installs and a few token changes in `index.css`, with no font files to commit. Fontshare fonts (General Sans, Zodiak, Gambetta) have to be downloaded and put in `public/`.

Choosing fonts from a table is hard. I can build a quick live switcher on the landing hero so you can flip between these on the real page and decide in a minute. Do you want that, or should I just apply one pairing?

content.text:
The wordmark is now Fraunces and `font-mono` is now Martian Mono. The production build passes, but I haven't looked at it running in the browser.

- **`src/main.tsx`**: replaced the Sora import with Fraunces (the full version with all axes) and Martian Mono.
- **`src/index.css`**:
  - `--font-brand` is now Fraunces.
  - I added the missing `--font-mono` token so `font-mono` actually uses Martian Mono, which fixes the bug from earlier.
  - The `.font-brand` class uses Fraunces's "Soft" setting at full and its quirky alternate letters turned off, which gives the round, warm lowercase look. I set the weight to 560 and the letter spacing to −0.025em; the old −0.035em was tuned for Sora and would crowd Fraunces's letters together.
- **`package.json`**: added the two new font packages and removed `@fontsource/sora`.

Two things to know:

1. **Martian Mono will hardly show up yet.** The only place using `font-mono` is the chart tooltip value in `chart.tsx:255`. For it to read as part of the style, readouts such as scores, compound IDs and percentages need the `font-mono` class. Martian Mono is wide, so check that nothing overflows when you add it.
2. **The ASCII background still uses Geist Mono**, because it names its font directly in `background.tsx:17`. I left it alone on purpose: Martian Mono's wider letters would change the background's character grid. Tell me if you want it switched too.

Nothing is committed yet. This branch (`frontend/live-agent`) has other uncommitted changes, so commit only `main.tsx`, `index.css`, `package.json` and `package-lock.json` if you want this kept separate. Run `npm run dev --prefix frontend` to see the new wordmark on the landing hero.

content.text:
Git didn't fail to resolve this. The automatic merge finished, but it left a broken result Git can't detect.

## What happened

From the reflog, the sequence was:

1. You stashed your live-agent work on `frontend/live-agent`.
2. You pulled `main`, which brought in **PR #25 (`frontend/profile-cards`)**, and fast-forwarded your branch onto it.
3. You ran `git stash pop` to bring your work back.

PR #25 and your stash both **rewrote `ProfilesPage` in `discovery/pages.tsx`**, in different ways:

- **main (PR #25):** replaced the inline grid with a new `<ProfileGrid />` component from `profile-card.tsx`, which has spotlight cards and entrance animations.
- **your stash:** kept the inline grid but made it live-agent aware. It uses `state.lanes` instead of the fixed `PROFILES`, a dynamic count ("N therapeutic hypotheses"), `p.criterion`, `strategies`, and a ranked trace.

Git flagged only the import line as a conflict, and I resolved that one. In the function body, your stash's version won and main's `<ProfileGrid />` call was dropped without any warning. So the file now imports `ProfileGrid` but never uses it, and **the build fails** (`TS6133: 'ProfileGrid' is declared but its value is never read`).

## Where things stand

- The conflict markers are gone and nothing is staged.
- `stash@{0}` still exists, because Git keeps a stash when popping it hits a conflict. Don't drop it until this is sorted.
- Every other file from the stash, including the font change, merged cleanly.

## You need to choose a version

This is a real design choice between your work and a teammate's merged PR, so I haven't picked one:

1. **Combine them (recommended).** Keep the new `ProfileGrid` cards, but have them read `state.lanes` and show your live fields (criterion, strategies, the dynamic count) instead of the fixed `PROFILES`. Then live runs get the new design. It's about 20–30 minutes of work in `profile-card.tsx`.
2. **Keep yours.** Delete the unused import. The build goes green immediately, but merging this branch would remove PR #25's cards from main.
3. **Keep main's.** Restore `ProfilesPage` from main. Live runs with more or fewer than five agents would then show the wrong count and miss your new fields.

Do you want me to do option 1? Whose code is `profile-card.tsx`? If it's a teammate's, check with them before I edit it, since the repo rules ask each file to have one owner.

* Start a research run (or replay a recorded one) and stream it as PipelineEvents.
 * `onEnd` fires once, with an error message if the run failed. Returns a cancel function.
 */
export function runLiveAgent(question: string, emit: (e: PipelineEvent) => void, onEnd: (error?: string) => void) {
  let es: EventSource | null = null
  let closed = false
  let ended = false
  const lanes = new Map<string, { lane: number; label: string; constraints: string[] }>()

  const end = (error?: string) => {
    if (ended) return
    ended = true
    es?.close()
    onEnd(error)
  }
  const step = (stage: 'analysis' | 'profiles', type: AgentStep['type'], label: string, content: string, lane?: number) =>
    emit({ type: 'step', stage, lane, step: { type, label, content } })

  function handle(e: AgentEvent) {
    const d = e.data ?? {}
    const lane = e.criterion ? lanes.get(e.criterion) : undefined
    switch (e.type) {
      case 'run_started':
        emit({ type: 'stage', stage: 'analysis', status: 'running' })
        step('analysis', 'output', 'Run started', `Orchestrator: ${d.models?.orchestrator}\nSub-agents: ${d.models?.subagent}\n\nQuestion: ${d.question}`)
        break
      case 'patient_loaded':
        step('analysis', 'tool_call', 'load_patient', json({ patient_id: d.patient_id }))
        step('analysis', 'tool_result', 'Patient record — result', `Loaded the record for "${d.patient_id}"${d.synthetic ? ' (synthetic)' : ''}.`)
        step('analysis', 'thinking', 'Planning the research', 'Reading the full record and choosing which disease mechanisms and symptoms to research for this patient. Sub-agents will only see a sanitised brief.')
        break
      case 'plan': {
        const briefs: { criterion: string; label: string; objective: string }[] = d.briefs ?? []
        briefs.forEach((b, i) => lanes.set(b.criterion, { lane: i, label: b.label, constraints: [] }))
        if (d.rationale) step('analysis', 'output', 'Research plan', d.rationale)
        // The orchestrator handing each brief to a sub-agent: that's the fan-out.
        briefs.forEach((b, i) => step('analysis', 'tool_call', `spawn_subagent · ${b.criterion} ${b.label}`, json({ criterion: b.criterion, objective: b.objective }), i))
        step('analysis', 'output', 'Privacy wall', `${briefs.length} briefs sent. ${d.redactions ?? 0} patient identifier${d.redactions === 1 ? '' : 's'} redacted before leaving the orchestrator.`)
        emit({ type: 'lanes', lanes: briefs.map((b, i) => ({ lane: i, name: b.label, criterion: b.criterion, objective: b.objective })) })
        emit({ type: 'stage', stage: 'analysis', status: 'done' })
        emit({ type: 'stage', stage: 'profiles', status: 'running' })
        break
      }
      case 'subagent_started':
        if (!lane) break
        lane.constraints = [...(d.constraints ?? []), ...(d.avoid ?? []).map((x: string) => `Avoid: ${x}`)]
        step('profiles', 'thinking', 'Brief received', `${d.objective}${lane.constraints.length ? `\n\n${lane.constraints.join('\n')}` : ''}`, lane.lane)
        break
      case 'tool_call':
        if (lane) step('profiles', 'tool_call', d.tool, json(d.args), lane.lane)
        break
      case 'tool_result':
        if (lane) step('profiles', 'tool_result', `${d.tool} — ${d.error ? 'error' : 'result'}`, `${Number(d.chars).toLocaleString()} characters returned${d.error ? ' (tool error)' : ''}.`, lane.lane)
        break
      case 'budget_exhausted':
        if (lane) step('profiles', 'thinking', 'Tool budget used', `Answering from the ${d.tool_results} results gathered so far.`, lane.lane)
        break
      case 'subagent_finished': {
        if (!lane) break
        const goals: string[] = d.goals ?? []
        const targets: string[][] = d.targets ?? []
        const profile: DrugProfile = {
          lane: lane.lane,
          name: lane.label,
          hypothesis: goals[0] ?? (d.dead_ends?.[0] ? `No profile: ${d.dead_ends[0]}` : 'No profile returned.'),
          targets: [...new Set(targets.flat())],
          modality: '',
          constraints: lane.constraints,
          strategies: goals.map((goal, i) => ({ goal, targets: targets[i] ?? [] })),
        }
        step('profiles', 'output', `${goals.length} profile${goals.length === 1 ? '' : 's'}`, goals.map((g, i) => `${i + 1}. ${g}`).join('\n') || (d.dead_ends ?? []).join('\n'), lane.lane)
        emit({ type: 'profile', profile })
        break
      }
      case 'verify':
        step('profiles', 'output', 'Evidence verified', `${d.kept} profiles kept · ${d.dropped_profiles} dropped · ${d.dropped_evidence} citations that don't exist removed · ${d.drug_mentions_removed} drug names scrubbed.`)
        break
      case 'report':
        step('profiles', 'output', 'Ranked for this patient', d.summary ?? '')
        emit({ type: 'stage', stage: 'profiles', status: 'done' })
        break
      case 'run_finished':
        end()
        break
      case 'error':
        end(d.message ?? 'The agent run failed.')
        break
    }
  }

  async function connect() {

The two versions are combined, and the build passes again. The profile cards from PR #25 now run on your live-agent data.

**`profile-card.tsx` (`ProfileGrid`):**
- It loops over `state.lanes` instead of the fixed `PROFILES`. A simulated run still gets the same five lanes, so the demo looks the same as before.
- The grid width follows the number of agents, using the column map I moved out of `pages.tsx`. Colours repeat after five lanes, so a 6th agent no longer gets an undefined colour.
- Each card header shows "Agent N · criterion" on live runs.
- When a live agent returns strategies, the card lists each goal with its targets, then the constraints. If an agent returns no strategies, the card shows its reason as written. The empty "Modality" row no longer appears on live profiles.
- On live runs the step labels are general ("Brief received / Tool calls / Evidence returned"). The open step view shows every tool call in a step, not just the first. Simulated runs keep the original labels.

**`pages.tsx` (`ProfilesPage`):** renders `<ProfileGrid />` again and keeps your dynamic count heading and the "Ranked for this patient" summary underneath.

The build passes, but I haven't looked at the page in a browser, either simulated or live. Click through the Profiles step once before you rely on it for the demo.

**Still to do:**
- **Drop the stash once you're happy:** `git stash drop`. Git keeps `stash@{0}` after a conflicted pop, and everything in it is now in your working tree.
- **Tell the owner of `profile-card.tsx`.** It's penguinyogurt28's file from PR #25, and I changed it fairly substantially. Mention that in your PR so they aren't surprised.
- **Nothing is committed.** The working tree still mixes the live-agent work, the font swap and this merge fix.

content.text:
Yes for the main agent backend, as long as you don't host the diagnostics models on the same box. I'm reading "1GB vCPU" as 1 vCPU. The RAM figures below are estimates from the code and data sizes; I didn't measure a real run.

## What the hosted backend runs

`backend/agent/` is the FastAPI server on :8001. A run has two parts:

1. **The research run** (LangGraph orchestrator plus sub-agents). The actual thinking happens at Anthropic, so your server mostly waits on network calls. It needs about 150–250 MB of RAM and very little CPU, even with `AGENT_MAX_CONCURRENCY=8`.
2. **DRKG scoring**: `agent/drkg.py` starts `frontend/scripts/drkg_scene.py` as a separate process for each run. This is the heavy part:
   - 5.87M knowledge-graph edges as integers: about 70 MB
   - Entity embeddings (97k × 400, float32): about 155 MB, memory-mapped so only the parts in use are loaded
   - Drug and gene vectors converted to float64, the lookup dicts, and Python/numpy itself: a few hundred MB more
   - **Estimated peak: about 0.4–0.7 GB per run**, for a few seconds of CPU work, because the layout and edge caches (`layout.npz`, `triples.npz`) are prebuilt

## Against your spec

| Resource | Need | Your spec | Verdict |
|---|---|---|---|
| RAM | about 1 GB with one DRKG run active | 2 GB | Fine for one or two people at a time. Add a 2 GB swap file in case two runs overlap. |
| CPU | DRKG scoring is the only CPU-heavy step | 1 vCPU | Fine. Scoring takes a little longer and two overlapping runs take turns, but the research run is limited by API speed, not CPU. |
| Storage | about 5 GB: 846 MB of DRKG data, a 1–2 GB virtualenv, and small per-run JSON files | 4 TB | Far more than you need. **20–40 GB is plenty**, and if you're paying for the 4 TB you can cut it. |

## When it wouldn't be enough

- **Hosting `backend/diagnostics/` too.** The speech scripts use PyTorch and PANNs, and the facial test uses MediaPipe. PyTorch plus a PANNs model can take 1–1.5 GB of RAM on its own, and inference on 1 vCPU would be slow. Keep diagnostics running locally (they're built as local servers) or put them on a box with 4 GB.
- **Missing DRKG caches.** If the `cache/` files aren't copied over, the first run has to read all 5.87M edges and rebuild the layout. That uses much more RAM and takes minutes on 1 vCPU. Copy `backend/.venv/data/drkg/` across whole, cache folder included, and the box never has to rebuild them.
- **Many simultaneous users.** Each extra DRKG run at the same moment adds about 0.5 GB. That's fine for an expo table, not for public traffic.

## Before deploying

- Add a swap file. It's cheap protection against an out-of-memory kill in the middle of the demo.
- Ship `backend/agent/.env` values through your host's secrets settings, not the file. In particular, `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` must never go in the image.
- The DRKG data currently sits inside `backend/.venv/`, which is an odd place for data. Point `DRKG_DIR` at a normal path on the server.

I can measure the real peak memory of one DRKG scoring run on your machine, which takes about a minute, so these numbers aren't just estimates. Want me to?

- the entity-details sidebar
- the search box

- the colour-by toggle and back/forward buttons

# Environment update
 - Primary working directory: C:\Users\jerem\BioHacks-2026\frontend (was C:\Users\jerem\BioHacks-2026\frontend\src\components\graph)

The graph now renders shifted to the right. The type legend in the bottom-left corner was covering part of it, so the graph now centres in the space to the legend's right. The build passes, but I haven't looked at it in the browser.

**The change** (`graph-canvas.tsx`, after the camera setup): a camera view offset slides what's drawn right by **118px**, half the legend's 236px footprint. On narrow canvases the shift is capped at 10% of the width. It's recalculated whenever the canvas resizes.

The camera itself doesn't move, so rotating still pivots around the graph's centre. Node labels and click targets move with the picture, so clicks still land on the right point.

**Side effect:** when you select a node, it also lands about 118px right of centre instead of dead centre. The legend collapses when something is selected, so that's slightly off-balance. If it bothers you, I can apply the offset only when nothing is selected.

**To adjust the amount:** change `118` in `Math.min(118, size.width * 0.1)`. A higher number moves the graph further right.

This is penguinyogurt28's file again, so it's one more thing to mention in your PR.
